Pressure (P=F⊥​/A)

 Home Physics Branches of physics Statistical physics Thermodynamics
OurBigBook.com Words: 7k Articles: 46
Pressure measures the compressive normal force per unit surface area. For a uniformly loaded surface of surface area A, the magnitude of the perpendicular force is F⊥​=PA; locally, P=dF⊥​/dA. Its SI unit is the pascal, 1Pa=1Nm−2. A force parallel to the surface contributes shear stress, rather than pressure. In a gas, the steady macroscopic force comes from many microscopic transfers of momentum; ideal gas pressure from wall collisions makes this connection explicit. [ref]
For a computed example, a uniform pressure of 100kPa on a piston of surface area 10cm2=10−3m2 produces a perpendicular force of 100N. If the opposite face is exposed to 80kPa, the net force due to the two pressures is (100−80)×103×10−3=20N, directed toward the lower-pressure side. The pressure on either face and their difference answer different questions; gauge pressure records a difference from a specified reference, often atmospheric pressure.
A scalar pressure describes a gas in local thermodynamic equilibrium with isotropic random particle velocities: every wall orientation has the same normal force per unit surface area. Without this isotropy, normal stresses can depend on direction and a pressure tensor is needed. Thus random motion alone is insufficient; a preferred direction matters.
In thermodynamics, pressure and volume are thermodynamic conjugate variables. For a simple compressible system, reversible expansion delivers work δW=PdV, and at fixed entropy S and particle number N,
P=−(∂V∂U​)S,N​,
(1)
where U is internal energy. A large pressure therefore means both a large wall force per unit surface area and a large amount of expansion work per small increase in volume.

Multi-anvil press

Words: 37
Pressure OurBigBook.com
A high-pressure apparatus in which several anvils compress a relatively large specimen. Compared with a diamond anvil cell, it typically offers greater sample volume for synthesis and bulk measurements, with less optical access and a lower ultimate pressure range.

Pressure sensor

Words: 34
Pressure OurBigBook.com
A pressure sensor converts a pressure into a recorded signal. An absolute pressure sensor uses a vacuum reference; a gauge pressure sensor uses a specified reference pressure. A closed gas syringe and an absolute pressure sensor can test Boyle's law after allowing the temperature to stabilize.

Atmospheric pressure (patm​)

Words: 48
Pressure OurBigBook.com
Atmospheric pressure often provides the reference for a gauge pressure measurement: pg​=pabs​−patm​. The absolute pressure is measured relative to an ideal vacuum, whereas zero gauge pressure means equality to the chosen reference. The actual atmospheric pressure can vary; it must be specified when converting between these descriptions. [ref].

Kinematic pressure (p/ρ0​)

Words: 33
Pressure OurBigBook.com
Dividing a pressure disturbance by the constant reference mass density ρ0​ gives a quantity whose gradient enters the Boussinesq equations directly as an acceleration. Its units are squared velocity. Distinguish this convention from physical pressure when calculating energy flux or comparing wave polarization formulae.

Pressure tensor (Pij​)

Words: 48
Pressure OurBigBook.com
In the local rest frame of a gas, the pressure tensor is the directional momentum flux Pij​=∫pi​vj​f(p)d3p, where f is the phase-space distribution function per unit momentum volume and v is particle velocity. For an isotropic distribution, Pij​=Pδij​, recovering the kinetic pressure of an isotropic gas. An anisotropic distribution can exert different normal pressures along different directions.

Radiation pressure (prad​)

Words: 1k Articles: 4
Pressure OurBigBook.com
Radiation pressure is the normal momentum flux transferred by electromagnetic radiation to a surface. A photon travelling in vacuum carries momentum pγ​=Eγ​/c=hν/c, where Eγ​ is its energy, ν its frequency, h the Planck constant and c the speed of light. Photon absorption transfers that momentum; specular reflection reverses its normal component. This lets light exert a force even when almost no energy becomes heat in the receiver.
Two useful formulas describe different preparations. A directed beam normally incident on a stationary perfect absorber gives pressure I/c, and on a stationary perfect mirror gives 2I/c. Here I is light intensity, the incident power per beam cross-sectional area perpendicular to propagation, in Wm−2. An isotropic photon gas has pressure u/3, where u=U/V is its radiation internal energy per volume, in Jm−3. Stored energy density and travelling energy flux must be distinguished: an isotropic field can have zero net energy flux and positive radiation pressure.
The physical appeal is that the same momentum conservation connects a single photon collision, a mirror's measurable force, and a radiation-filled cavity's equation of state. The directional calculation below complements radiation pressure on a perfectly absorbing surface; the equilibrium spectrum and its temperature dependence belong to blackbody radiation and the photon gas.

Proper-time acceleration by reflected laser light (β(τ)=τ/(τ+τ0​))

Words: 56
Radiation pressure OurBigBook.com
An ideal receding mirror reflecting a source beam of constant power P receives force (2P/c)(1−β)/(1+β) after including both Doppler-shifted reflected momentum and reduced impact rate. For fixed rest mass M, use dt/dτ=γ in the momentum equation. It reduces to dβ/dτ=(1−β)2/τ0​, where τ0​=Mc2/(2P). Starting from rest gives β=τ/(τ+τ0​). This continuum mirror model neglects individual-photon recoil and finite beam interception.

Radiation pressure of a directed beam (p⊥​=(a+2R)Icos2θ/c)

Words: 376
Radiation pressure OurBigBook.com
For normal incidence in vacuum, a uniform beam delivers energy IAΔt to an illuminated surface area A during time Δt. A perfect absorber receives momentum IAΔt/c, so force divided by surface area gives pabs​=I/c. A perfect stationary mirror sends the photons back with reversed momentum, so momentum conservation gives twice the normal transfer, prefl​=2I/c. These are time-averaged pressures; the microscopic arrivals need not be uniform.
For a stipulated model light intensity I=1000Wm−2 and the exact SI speed of light c=299792458ms−1,
pabs​=3.335640952×10−6Pa≃3.3356μPa,prefl​=6.671281904×10−6Pa≃6.6713μPa.
(2)
These are computed predictions, not measured data or a universal sunlight value. If the beam fully covers a normally oriented surface area A=0.010m2, the intercepted radiant flux is Φ=IA=10W and the absorber's force is Φ/c≃33.356nN. Using the total source power would be wrong if only part of its beam reaches the receiver. The absorption prediction assumes complete photon absorption, while the reflection prediction assumes complete specular reflection; transmission, scattering of light and directed thermal photon emission require their own outgoing momentum accounting.
Measure the angle of incidence θ between the incoming path and the surface's normal line, with 0≤θ<π/2. There are two separate cosine factors. A fixed actual surface area A intercepts only its projected area Acosθ, so Φ=IAcosθ. Each incoming photon supplies normal momentum (Eγ​/c)cosθ on absorption, or twice that on specular reflection. Thus, for radiometric absorptance a and reflected power fraction R,
F⊥​=(a+2R)cΦ​cosθ,p⊥​=AF⊥​​=(a+2R)cI​cos2θ.
(3)
This model assumes transmitted light continues straight in the same medium and carries away its original momentum. It omits thermal recoil and assumes a stationary receiver. At θ=60∘, fixed beam light intensity therefore gives one quarter of the normal-incidence pressure. For fixed intercepted radiant flux Φ, however, the normal force has only one cosine factor. Equivalently, if the given quantity is receiving-surface irradiance Einc​=Icosθ, then p⊥​=(a+2R)Einc​cosθ/c. The distinction matters when interpreting an experiment's angle scan. [ref]
Absorption also transfers a tangential momentum component at oblique incidence. It contributes a tangential force, rather than normal pressure. Ideal specular reflection preserves the tangential momentum component, so it transfers only normal momentum.

Radiation pressure of an isotropic photon gas (prad​=u/3)

Words: 300
Radiation pressure OurBigBook.com
For radiation in vacuum with isotropy, energy is distributed equally per solid angle: write uΩ​=u/(4π) for energy density per unit solid angle. Let θ be the angle between a ray's path and the wall normal. Its normal velocity ccosθ determines the arrival rate, while normal momentum per energy is cosθ/c. Their product is cos2θ. For a perfectly reflecting cavity wall,
prad​=2∫incoming hemisphere​uΩ​cos2θdΩ=4π2u​∫02π​dφ∫0π/2​cos2θsinθdθ=3u​.
(4)
The leading two is the normal momentum reversal; the incoming hemisphere contains half of the field's directional energy density. This is also the normal component of the bulk pressure tensor, Pnn​=∫4π​uΩ​cos2θdΩ=u/3. Isotropy makes all three diagonal components equal, while their sum is u because the squared direction components sum to one. The factor one third therefore depends on three-dimensional angular geometry, not on the shape of the blackbody radiation spectrum.
A perfectly absorbing wall exposed to this incoming hemisphere receives only u/6 from absorption. If it is in thermal equilibrium with the isotropic radiation, its outgoing emission supplies another u/6 of recoil, recovering u/3. A cold absorber before equilibrium is a different boundary condition. Similarly, the one-way incident energy flux is cu/4, whereas the net energy flux across a plane in the undisturbed isotropic field is zero. Dividing cu/4 by c misses the extra normal-momentum projection and does not give the cavity pressure.
For a stipulated isotropic radiation energy density u=6μJm−3, the bulk pressure is 2μPa regardless of its spectral shape. In thermal equilibrium, blackbody radiation supplies u=arad​T4 with radiation constant arad​=4σ/c, so prad​=arad​T4/3; Stefan–Boltzmann law defines σ. The equilibrium photon gas derives this same equation of state from its free energy.[ref]

Radiation-pressure laser power measurement (Φ=cF⊥​/[(a+2R)cosθ])

Words: 182
Radiation pressure OurBigBook.com
A 2013 experiment by Paul A. Williams and collaborators mounted a 25-mm dielectric mirror on a commercial force-restoration balance. Removing its pan-weight compensation spring allowed horizontal force sensing with a horizontal laser path. They measured mirror optical reflectance and varied incidence from about 7∘ to 45∘. A 1071-nm laser, capable of 530 W, was switched at 0.1 Hz. Digitized mass-equivalent readings were converted to force using g; quadrature demodulation isolated the switched signal from drift. [ref]
Measurement calibration used a 20-g mass, with checks down to 1 mg. The optical forces lay below that checked range, limiting the accuracy claim. An angle scan tested the predicted cosine dependence at fixed intercepted power. Replacing the mirror with a carbon nanotube coated absorber increased absorbed power while reducing the predicted optical force; no modulation peak was detected. This bounded gas-heating artifacts under those conditions, rather than proving their universal absence. The fitted slope was about 7% below 2/c. Inferring laser power requires calibrated force, optical reflectance, radiometric absorptance and angle of incidence, with measurement uncertainty for each. [ref]

Pressure OurBigBook.com
An equation of state is a relation among thermodynamic state variables such as pressure, volume, temperature, energy, and particle number.

Compressibility factor (Z=p/(nkB​T))

Words: 38
Equation of state OurBigBook.com
The compressibility factor is the ratio p/(nkB​T), where n is number density. A classical ideal gas has Z=1. The virial expansion writes Z=1+B2​n+B3​n2+⋯ for a dilute gas; this dimensionless ratio is distinct from isothermal compressibility, which is a response derivative with units of inverse pressure.

Barotropic stellar equation of state (p=p(ρ))

Words: 45
Equation of state OurBigBook.com
A perfect fluid in general relativity stellar model in which pressure depends only on energy density, p=p(ρ). A positive derivative makes this relation locally invertible and turns outward-decreasing pressure into outward-decreasing density. This general relation need not have the constant ratio p/ρ used for a constant cosmological fluid parameter.

Clausius gas

Words: 21
Equation of state OurBigBook.com
A Clausius gas with covolume parameter b obeys P(V−Nb)=NkB​T. It is the repulsive-volume part of a Van der Waals equation without the attractive term.

Van der Waals equation

Words: 2k Articles: 14
Equation of state OurBigBook.com
The Van der Waals equation is a simple real gas equation of state that can also describe a liquid-gas critical point. With particle count N fixed, write the volume per particle as v=V/N:
p=v−bkB​T​−v2a​,v>b,a>0,b>0,
(5)
or equivalently (p+aN2/V2)(V−Nb)=NkB​T. Here p is pressure, T is absolute temperature, and kB​ is the Boltzmann constant. In SI, v and b have units m3 per particle, a has units Pam6=Jm3, and kB​ has units JK−1; the particle count is dimensionless. The pole at v=b excludes smaller volume values from this model.
The b correction represents excluded volume; the attraction term lowers pressure at fixed temperature and particle number density 1/v. This is a mean-field theory, replacing detailed intermolecular structure by two parameters. At v≫b with a/v2≪kB​T/v, it approaches the ideal gas law pv=kB​T. It supplies a useful qualitative route from a dilute gas to phase coexistence, without a claim of quantitative accuracy for every fluid.[ref]
Do not mix this particle convention with the molar volume convention elsewhere in this article. With amount of substance nmol​=N/NA​, Avogadro constant NA​, and molar gas constant R=NA​kB​, one has vm​=NA​v, bm​=NA​b, and am​=NA2​a, so p=RT/(vm​−bm​)−am​/vm2​. The molar parameters have units m3mol−1 and Pam6mol−2, respectively.
Johannes Diderik van der Waals introduced this equation of state in 1873, connecting molecular attraction with departures from the dilute ideal gas law. Its historical significance is the unified treatment of gases and liquids, rather than a universally exact fit.[ref]

Van der Waals gas

Words: 86 Articles: 1
Van der Waals equation OurBigBook.com
A mean-field fluid model with excluded-volume and attractive-interaction parameters, described by the Van der Waals equation. Its pressure law alone does not fix every thermal property: the caloric closure of the van der Waals equation supplies the additional internal-energy assumption.
Isothermal free-energy change of a Van der Waals gas (ΔF=−RTln[(V2​−b)/(V1​−b)]+a(1/V1​−1/V2​))
Words: 57
Van der Waals gas OurBigBook.com
For the one-mole Van der Waals equation with constant parameters, integrate dF=−pdV along an isotherm to obtain the displayed difference. The attractive contribution has a positive change on expansion, whereas the translational term lowers free energy. Thermodynamic consistency independently gives ΔU=a(1/V1​−1/V2​) and ΔS=Rln[(V2​−b)/(V1​−b)]. These homogeneous-branch expressions are not a substitute for equilibrium convexification through a subcritical coexistence region.

Caloric closure of the van der Waals equation

Words: 30
Van der Waals equation OurBigBook.com
The thermodynamic identity (∂U/∂V)T​=T(∂P/∂T)V​−P fixes the volume-dependent term −aN2/V but leaves an arbitrary function of temperature. Classical monatomic mean-field modelling adds 3NkB​T/2, giving U=3NkB​T/2−aN2/V+C.

Internal energy of a van der Waals gas (U(V,T)=h(T)−a/V)

Words: 102
Van der Waals equation OurBigBook.com
For fixed amount of substance, thermodynamic consistency gives
(∂V∂U​)T​=T(∂T∂P​)V​−P.
(6)
Indeed, the first law of thermodynamics gives UV​∣T​=TSV​∣T​−P, and the Helmholtz free energy Maxwell relation gives SV​∣T​=PT​∣V​. For the fixed-amount convention P=RT/(V−b)−a/V2 with temperature-independent a,b, substitution gives UV​∣T​=a/V2. Integration yields U=h(T)−a/V. If the dilute-limit reference is U→cT as V→∞ for every T, then h(T)=cT.
The same formula may be interpreted molarly if V,U,a,b all use that convention. Mixing molar and total quantities changes the amount factors. The attraction controls the volume correction to internal energy, while excluded volume alone does not contribute to this derivative when a,b are independent of temperature.

Entropy excess of a van der Waals gas (ΔSex=Rln(1−b/V))

Words: 65
Van der Waals equation OurBigBook.com
For one mole with temperature-independent parameters a,b, the equation of state is P=RT/(V−b)−a/V2. A Maxwell relation gives (∂S/∂V)T​=R/(V−b), so the volume dependence is Rln(V−b). Matching the ideal gas entropy at infinite volume fixes the excess at the same V,T to Rln(1−b/V). The attraction contributes −a/V to the Helmholtz free energy but no excess entropy when a is independent of temperature. A temperature-dependent attraction parameter would change this conclusion.

Van der Waals molar equation (p=RT/(vm​−bm​)−am​/vm2​)

Words: 538 Articles: 1
Van der Waals equation OurBigBook.com
The molar volume vm​=V/nmol​ is the volume per amount of substance, not the total container volume or the volume per particle. In the molar convention of the Van der Waals equation, take constant positive parameters
[am​]=Pam6mol−2,[bm​]=m3mol−1,[R]=Pam3mol−1K−1.
(7)
Then
p=vm​−bm​RT​−vm2​am​​,vm​>bm​,
(8)
or, for any fixed amount of substance,
(p+V2am​nmol2​​)(V−nmol​bm​)=nmol​RT.
(9)
Both terms in the first equation are pressures. The total excluded volume is nmol​bm​: using V−bm​ would subtract quantities with different units. Changing the sample size at fixed molar volume and temperature changes V and nmol​ proportionally, while leaving pressure unchanged. This is a useful unit and extensivity check before fitting a real gas.
For the molar Van der Waals critical point, differentiate with respect to molar volume at fixed temperature:
(∂vm​∂p​)T​=−(vm​−bm​)2RT​+vm3​2am​​,(∂vm2​∂2p​)T​=(vm​−bm​)32RT​−vm4​6am​​.
(10)
Setting both to zero gives RTc​=2am​(vm,c​−bm​)2/vm,c3​ and RTc​=3am​(vm,c​−bm​)3/vm,c4​. Equating them and dividing by the nonzero factors yields 2vm,c​=3(vm,c​−bm​), so
vm,c​=3bm​,Tc​=27Rbm​8am​​,pc​=27bm2​am​​.
(11)
Here vm,c​ has units m3mol−1, Tc​ has units K, and pc​ has units Pa. This is the molar version of the particle derivation below: vm,c​=NA​vc​, with the same physical Tc​ and pc​. If one writes vc​=3b, Tc​=8a/(27Rb) and pc​=a/(27b2) without subscripts, then all of vc​,b,a in those formulas must be molar quantities.
Now define the dimensionless reduced variables explicitly as x=vm​/vm,c​, t=T/Tc​ and q=p/pc​. Substituting the three critical values cancels am​,bm​,R and gives
q=3x−18t​−x23​.
(12)
Because vm​/vm,c​=v/vc​, these are exactly the reduced variables in the Van der Waals isotherm discussion. The Van der Waals law of corresponding states is therefore independent of whether one starts with particle or molar units. It predicts a critical ratio pc​vm,c​/(RTc​)=3/8, providing a third check on any proposed parameter fit.
Molar Van der Waals worked example
Words: 278
Van der Waals molar equation OurBigBook.com
Choose a hypothetical fluid with molar constants am​=0.360Pam6mol−2 and bm​=4.00×10−5m3mol−1, using R=8.314462618Jmol−1K−1. These stipulated constants are not a fit to carbon dioxide. The molar critical formulas give
vm,c​=120.0cm3mol−1,Tc​≃320.7263K,pc​=8.333333MPa.
(13)
At T=360K and vm​=240cm3mol−1, first convert vm​ to 2.40×10−4m3mol−1. The repulsive-volume term and attractive correction are
vm​−bm​RT​=14.966033MPa,vm2​am​​=6.250000MPa,
(14)
so p=8.716033MPa. The ideal gas law would instead give RT/vm​=12.471694MPa. The excluded volume raises pressure relative to that ideal value, but attraction more than offsets the increase here. Neither correction alone describes this example.
For nmol​=0.500mol, the same state occupies V=nmol​vm​=120cm3. The total-volume formula gives nmol​bm​=20cm3 and the same 8.716033MPa. Halving the sample has halved both its physical volume and its excluded volume, while retaining its pressure. Conversely, if the two critical measurements Tc​,pc​ are used to determine model constants, inversion gives
bm​=8pc​RTc​​,am​=64pc​27R2Tc2​​.
(15)
An independent critical molar volume then tests the prediction vm,c​=3RTc​/(8pc​); agreement with two fitted numbers does not ensure agreement with the third.
At t=0.9, the Van der Waals liquid-gas coexistence example below becomes T≃288.6537K, p∗​≃5.391653MPa, vm,l​≃72.40823cm3mol−1 and vm,g​≃281.8611cm3mol−1. For a mean molar volume of 120cm3mol−1, the lever rule gives gas mole fraction fg​≃0.227219. Its volume fraction is instead fg​vm,g​/vm​≃0.533703: less than one quarter of the molecules occupy more than half the volume. The flat equilibrium pressure corresponds to changing these proportions. It does not describe a homogeneous sample sliding along the unstable loop.

Van der Waals law of corresponding states

Words: 40
Van der Waals equation OurBigBook.com
The Van der Waals equation becomes independent of its material parameters when pressure, temperature and molecular volume are divided by their critical values: pˉ​=8Tˉ/(3vˉ−1)−3/vˉ2. This explains the common reduced isotherms within this model, without claiming exact agreement for all real fluids.

Van der Waals isotherm (p(v,T))

Words: 171
Van der Waals equation OurBigBook.com
A Van der Waals isotherm is the pressure–particle volume curve at a fixed temperature. Put x=v/vc​, t=T/Tc​, and q=p/pc​, using the Van der Waals critical point values below. Then the existing Van der Waals law of corresponding states becomes
q(x,t)=3x−18t​−x23​,x>31​.
(16)
All curves in the figure are calculations in this reduced model.
For a uniform thermodynamic phase, the isothermal compressibility is
κT​=−v1​(∂p∂v​)T​=−v(∂p/∂v)T​1​.
(17)
Thus the upward-sloping portion of a subcritical Van der Waals isotherm has κT​<0: compression would reduce pressure, allowing a density disturbance to grow. It is mechanically unstable. The spinodal points bound that portion; setting the derivative ∂q/∂x to zero gives their curve t=(3x−1)2/(4x3). Negative slope alone guarantees only local mechanical stability: portions between the spinodal and the phase coexistence endpoints have metastability. Equilibrium replaces the entire interval between those endpoints, including these metastable portions, by a Maxwell construction plateau.[ref]

Van der Waals critical point ((vc​,Tc​,pc​))

Words: 182 Articles: 1
Van der Waals equation OurBigBook.com
The liquid-gas critical point of the Van der Waals equation occurs where its two subcritical stationary points merge into a horizontal inflection point. The conditions are (∂p/∂v)T​=(∂2p/∂v2)T​=0. The short calculation is
−(vc​−b)2kB​Tc​​+vc3​2a​=0,(vc​−b)32kB​Tc​​−vc4​6a​=0.
(18)
Dividing these relations gives 2/(vc​−b)=3/vc​, hence
vc​=3b,Tc​=27bkB​8a​,pc​=27b2a​.
(19)
Substitution gives the Van der Waals law of corresponding states and the parameter-independent ratio pc​vc​/(kB​Tc​)=3/8. That ratio belongs to this equation of state; reducing a real fluid's variables does not enforce it.[ref]
An exact rearrangement of the reduced critical Van der Waals isotherm makes its flatness visible:
q(x,1)−1=−x2(3x−1)3(x−1)3​.
(20)
The first nonzero departure near x=1 is −3(x−1)3/2. On the critical particle volume approached from t>1, (∂q/∂x)x=1​=−6(t−1) and
κT​=6pc​(t−1)1​.
(21)
The divergent isothermal compressibility and cubic flattening explain why the critical region is mechanically soft. These are mean-field theory predictions; thermal fluctuations limit their use for real fluids very close to a thermodynamic critical point.
Critical-isochore compressibility of a van der Waals gas (κT​=4b/[3R(T−Tc​)])
Words: 49
Van der Waals critical point OurBigBook.com
For molar equation p=RT/(v−b)−a/v2, the critical values are vc​=3b and Tc​=8a/(27Rb). At v=vc​, (∂p/∂v)T​=−R(T−Tc​)/(4b2). Thus κT​=−vc−1​(∂v/∂p)T​=4b/[3R(T−Tc​)] on the stable branch above Tc​. The mean-field compressibility exponent is one; the continuation below the critical temperature is unstable rather than an equilibrium negative compressibility.

Van der Waals liquid-gas coexistence

Words: 443 Articles: 1
Van der Waals equation OurBigBook.com
Below Tc​, the equilibrium liquid and gas have the same temperature, pressure p∗​, and per-particle chemical potential. For macroscopic bulk thermodynamic phases, neglect interface contributions. The Maxwell equal-area construction determines vl​ and vg​ by
p(vl​,T)=p(vg​,T)=p∗​,∫vl​vg​​[p(v,T)−p∗​]dv=0.
(22)
It expresses equality of chemical potentials, since dμ=vdp at fixed temperature. Equivalently, the equilibrium Helmholtz free energy per particle follows a common tangent line between the two endpoint states, lying below the homogeneous continuation between them. The construction uses that mathematical continuation to compare endpoints; it is not a physical compression path through negative isothermal compressibility states.[ref]
Here is a reproducible calculated example at t=0.9. With q∗​=p∗​/pc​, the homogeneous intersections solve the cubic equation
3q∗​x3−(q∗​+8t)x2+9x−3=0.
(23)
The Maxwell construction gives
q∗​≃0.646998352,(xl​,xm​,xg​)≃(0.603401903, 1.090526633, 2.348842376).
(24)
All three roots of a polynomial satisfy x>1/3. Only the smallest and largest are the phase coexistence endpoints; the middle one has negative isothermal compressibility. Equal pressures at three admissible values of volume therefore do not imply three stable thermodynamic phases. An analytic area check is
38t​ln3xl​−13xg​−1​+3(xg​1​−xl​1​)−q∗​(xg​−xl​)=0.
(25)
At full numerical precision, the residual is below 10−11 in reduced units; independent numerical integration gives the same cancellation. At t=0.9, the spinodal points are instead x≃0.718597189 and 1.528504964.
The equilibrium plateau changes the phase fraction rather than the endpoint densities. For a gas particle fraction fg​=Ng​/N and mean particle volume vˉ=V/N, the lever rule reads
vˉ=(1−fg​)vl​+fg​vg​,fg​=vg​−vl​vˉ−vl​​.
(26)
Thus vˉ=vc​ at t=0.9 gives fg​≃0.227219: this is a particle fraction, not the volume fraction occupied by gas. Differentiating equality of chemical potentials along this model's phase coexistence curve yields the same Clapeyron equation explained below, dp∗​/dT=ℓ/[T(vg​−vl​)], with latent heat ℓ per particle. Both endpoint differences vanish as the Van der Waals critical point is approached; the equation's critical limit must be taken as a ratio.
The Maxwell construction presumes a pure bulk fluid at thermodynamic equilibrium. Its endpoint equality does not specify how rapidly a real compression reaches equilibrium. A homogeneous metastable sample can persist while nucleation is delayed; the spinodal marks loss of local mechanical stability in this mean-field theory, rather than the equilibrium onset of condensation. Surface tension, finite sample size and impurities can affect the observed transition. These qualifications matter when comparing a mathematical Van der Waals isotherm with a visible liquid meniscus.
Low-temperature liquid volume of a van der Waals gas (Vl​∼b+RTb2/a)
Words: 61
Van der Waals liquid-gas coexistence OurBigBook.com
For one mole, liquid–vapour phase coexistence requires equal pressure and chemical potential. At τ=RTb/a≪1, the saturation pressure is exponentially small. Neglecting it in the dense-phase equation of state gives RTVl2​−aVl​+ab=0. The root near the excluded volume is
Vl​≃2RTa​(1−1−4RTb/a​)=1+1−4τ​2b​=b(1+τ+2τ2+⋯).
(27)
This is an asymptotic low-temperature result, not an exact coexistence volume at every subcritical temperature. Away from that limit, solve equal pressure together with the Maxwell equal-area construction.

Andrews's carbon dioxide experiment

Words: 375
Van der Waals equation OurBigBook.com
The 1869 The Bakerian Lecture: On the Continuity of the Gaseous and Liquid States of Matter by Thomas Andrews describes dried carbon dioxide trapped above mercury in a sealed capillary tube. A steel screw pressurized water in a strong copper tube; movable mercury transmitted the load. A second capillary tube held air as a pressure gauge. Flowing water around the visible capillary tubes controlled temperature; a thermometer read the bath. A cathetometer read column positions, converted to volume readings using weighed-mercury calibration.[ref]
Below the critical temperature, compression produced a visible liquid–gas boundary; above it, large density changes occurred without that boundary. Three trials gave 30.92∘C as his critical temperature. Purity checks detected residual air; mercury height corrections accounted for unequal hydrostatic pressures. He explicitly left air nonideality and pressure-induced tube-capacity corrections unresolved, so his air-gauge pressures were approximate. These readouts support a liquid-gas critical point; they do not measure a homogeneous unstable loop or establish universal quantitative accuracy of the later Van der Waals equation.[ref]
A disappearing liquid meniscus by itself has more than one possible explanation: in ordinary subcritical condensation or evaporation, one thermodynamic phase can simply run out. The stronger critical-point inference combines temperature control, compression readings and the existence of a continuous route around the endpoint of the phase coexistence curve. On that route a dilute gas can become dense without crossing a two-phase boundary. This is what continuity of liquid and gas means; it does not remove their distinct equilibrium number densities below Tc​.
In his 12 December 1910 Nobel lecture, Johannes Diderik van der Waals explained gases and liquids through the same moving molecules, with attraction and finite size modifying their pressure. He also rejected the idea that constant a,b should give universal numerical agreement. His critical-volume discussion explicitly retained derivatives of a volume-dependent b: the familiar vc​=3b follows only when those derivatives are neglected. Thus the elegant constant-parameter Van der Waals critical point is a model result whose limitations were already part of its author's account.[ref]

Pressure measurement

Words: 3k Articles: 13
Pressure OurBigBook.com
A pressure measurement determines pressure relative to a specified reference using an instrument such as a manometer or pressure transducer. Gauge pressure, absolute pressure and differential pressure require different references; measurement calibration and measurement uncertainty determine how the reading can be interpreted.

High-pressure experimental metrology

Words: 3k Articles: 12
Pressure measurement OurBigBook.com
High-pressure experimental metrology connects three tasks: producing pressure, retaining it without leakage, and assigning a calibrated value to the pressure experienced by a sample. A large applied force alone establishes none of the last two. The useful result is a reproducible material property at specified pressure, temperature and stress conditions, with stated measurement uncertainty.
Percy Williams Bridgman identified leakage as an earlier experimental limit. His 1946 lecture describes packing that tightens as pressure rises, ultimately leaving vessel strength as a limit.[ref]
The Bridgman unsupported-area seal turns the very pressure that would drive a leak into an extra seating force. Its appeal is a feedback between load and sealing, rather than an assumption of perfectly fitted rigid surfaces. The piston-cylinder pressure apparatus below explains that feedback; pressure calibration then separates the applied load from the sample's inferred pressure.

Piston-cylinder pressure apparatus (p−pext​≃F/A)

Words: 544 Articles: 1
High-pressure experimental metrology OurBigBook.com
In a functional model, a driven piston reduces the chamber's volume. A surrounding cylinder carries the wall stress; a deformable packing or gasket closes a potential leak path around a moving or removable closure. A sample and a separate pressure sensor occupy the chamber. A transmitting liquid can load the sample on all sides; the sensor's signal passes to an external readout. This is a division of experimental functions, not a scale reconstruction of one historical machine.
For a slowly moving frictionless drive piston of effective surface area A, external pressure pext​ and inward applied force F, Newton's second law at mechanical balance gives
F+pext​A−pA=0,p−pext​=F/A.
(29)
Thus 20kN on a stipulated 20mm2 effective surface area corresponds ideally to 1GPa of differential pressure. These are illustrative numbers, not apparatus specifications. The effective surface area is the one associated with the pressure difference, not necessarily an external ram's visible cross section. With resisting friction Ff​ during inward motion, the balance becomes p−pext​=(F−Ff​)/A. During outward motion the sign of the friction contribution reverses. An applied-load reading can therefore show hysteresis even when the chamber's actual pressure is well defined.
A resistance pressure gauge instead supplies an internal signal. In a generic electrical readout, measure an electric potential difference Ve​ with a known electric current I and use Ohm's law to infer electrical resistance R=Ve​/I. This describes a possible readout principle; the lecture passage cited below identifies the sensor material and calibration landmarks without specifying this wiring.
Bridgman unsupported-area seal (q=pAp​/Aseal​)
Words: 326
Piston-cylinder pressure apparatus OurBigBook.com
Consider an ideal pressure-driven closure plug with a large chamber-facing projected area Ap​. Its opposite side seats against a smaller annular packing surface area Aseal​. The remaining projected part Au​=Ap​−Aseal​>0 is the unsupported area: it has no opposing packing contact in that plane. Here p is the chamber pressure relative to the exterior. Let q denote the mean axial compressive contact stress on the packing, not the chamber's hydrostatic stress.
Neglect friction, the plug's weight, and other axial reactions. The plug's Newton's second law in static balance is
pAp​−qAseal​=0,q=pAseal​Ap​​=p(1+Aseal​Au​​)>p.
(30)
The load is the same on both sides; its smaller supporting surface area raises the packing's mean contact stress. For a stipulated ratio Ap​/Aseal​=1.25 and p=1GPa, the ideal seating stress is q=1.25GPa. Its excess over chamber pressure is 0.25GPa. Reducing Au​ to zero removes this amplification. This is the elementary force balance behind self-energizing seating, consistent with the lecture's Figure 1 caption.[ref]
The relation is a model, not a universal sealing law. The mean axial contact stress need not equal the local contact stress along every possible leakage path. Confinement and plasticity in continuum mechanics determine whether the packing closes a gap or instead extrudes into it. Friction diverts load into other surfaces; material plasticity in continuum mechanics changes contact geometry; the vessel must carry its own stress. A finite initial seating load may also be needed before chamber pressure can develop. An arbitrarily small Aseal​ does not yield arbitrarily useful sealing: the assumptions fail when local deformation, extrusion or structural failure takes over.

Hydrostatic stress (σ=−pI)

Words: 178
High-pressure experimental metrology OurBigBook.com
With tension taken positive, hydrostatic stress is the stress tensor σ=−pI, where I is the identity matrix. Every plane has the same compressive normal stress, and no tangential traction. More generally,
p=−31​trσ,σ=−pI+s,trs=0,
(31)
where s is deviatoric stress. Two samples can share the same mean pressure while experiencing different deviatoric stresses. A stationary liquid cannot sustain equilibrium shear stress; a solid transmitting medium can support it. Consequently, a load divided by surface area does not by itself establish hydrostatic sample conditions. A transmitting medium's state at the actual pressure and temperature, and contact between sample and walls, matter.
Bridgman's Figure 4 compares mild steel fractured in tension at atmospheric pressure with steel stretched further in a liquid at 25000kgfcm−2.[ref] The imposed tension remains a directional load: the experiment combines confinement with deformation, rather than measuring a hydrostatic stress alone. Its comparison motivates recording the loading path and the surrounding medium as well as pressure; it does not establish a universal fracture threshold for all steels.

Pressure calibration (p=g(R,T,history))

Words: 466 Articles: 1
High-pressure experimental metrology OurBigBook.com
Pressure calibration assigns pressure values to a sensor's output by comparison with a reference under specified conditions. It is not the same as making the output more finely resolved. A smooth electrical resistance curve can be repeatable yet have an incorrect pressure scale.
Bridgman used pressure-dependent electrical resistance of manganin and established fixed points, including a bismuth transition. He reported poorer accuracy above the better calibrated range.[ref]
A fixed-point specimen and a property-measurement sample have distinct roles: one helps assign the scale, while the other is studied on that scale. The reference transition must itself have an assigned pressure at the relevant temperature. Agreement at a single point does not determine a nonlinear sensor response elsewhere. Comparing increasing and decreasing pressure checks hysteresis; returning to a reference checks drift. These are checks one can design from the measurement model, not additional historical controls asserted for the lecture's experiments.
Resistance pressure gauge (R=R(p,T,history))
Words: 312
Pressure calibration OurBigBook.com
A resistance pressure gauge is a pressure sensor whose electrical resistance is calibrated against pressure. Even a simple local response needs both pressure and temperature. For an original illustrative model define
y=R0​R​−1=αp+β(T−T0​)+h,p=αy−β(T−T0​)−h​,
(32)
where R0​ is the reference electrical resistance at p=0, T=T0​, and zero history offset. The derivatives α and β are local sensitivities with units Pa−1 and K−1, respectively; h is a dimensionless history offset. Constant sensitivities are an approximation over a chosen range, not material constants valid at every pressure.
Choose synthetic coefficients α=0.020GPa−1 and β=2.0×10−4K−1, with T−T0​=10K and h=0. A measured ratio R/R0​=1.022 then gives p=(0.022−0.002)/0.020=1.00GPa. Ignoring the temperature change gives 1.10GPa, a 0.10GPa error. This model is deliberately stipulated; these numbers are not measured manganin coefficients or Bridgman's data.
If two histories differ by Δh=0.0004, their outputs at the same pressure differ by 0.0004R0​; interpreting both with a single history-free curve gives an apparent pressure separation Δh/α=0.020GPa. The half separation is 0.010GPa. Reversing the drive can additionally cause mechanical friction hysteresis, independently of this sensor model. Record both the electrical calibration history and the loading direction.
For independent small standard measurement uncertainties uy​,uT​,uh​ and exact stipulated α,β, first-order propagation gives
up2​=α2uy2​+β2uT2​+uh2​​.
(33)
For uy​=10−4, uT​=0.5K, and uh​=10−4, this is up​=0.00866GPa. Real calibration also includes coefficient measurement uncertainties, correlations, reference-point measurement uncertainty, and any unresolved nonhydrostatic loading. A sensor calibrates its local environment; it cannot by itself certify the absence of deviatoric stress throughout the sample.

Diamond anvil cell

Words: 1k Articles: 6
High-pressure experimental metrology OurBigBook.com
A diamond anvil cell compresses a sample between opposed diamond tips. The flat diamond anvil culets load a metal gasket whose hole holds the specimen and a pressure-transmitting medium. Transparent diamond admits excitation and returning fluorescence, enabling an internal ruby pressure sensor.[ref]
The functions in the drawing answer different questions. The drive applies force, the gasket confines the sample, the medium transmits stress, and the ruby pressure scale assigns a local pressure from an optical signal. A large drive reading cannot establish either the sample's pressure or the absence of deviatoric stress. Optical access also permits repeated readings without unloading the sample: a change during a long measurement can be detected rather than silently folded into a material-property curve.
Diamond anvil culet (Ac​=πdc2​/4)
Words: 205
Diamond anvil cell OurBigBook.com
A diamond anvil culet is the small flat contact face at the tip of a diamond anvil. Its diameter dc​ determines its nominal surface area Ac​. The gasket hole has a different surface area Ah​; neither should be confused with the much larger drive mechanism. For an ideal static axial balance, F is the compressive force on either anvil. The two equal opposing loads do not produce 2F through a single contact.
For an original chosen geometry, F=1000N and dc​=0.300mm give
Ac​=7.0686×10−8m2,qˉ​=F/Ac​=14.147GPa.
(34)
Here qˉ​ is the mean axial contact stress over the culet, not a measured chamber pressure. Using a 0.100mm hole instead would give F/Ah​=127.324GPa, nine times larger. That substitution falsely assigns the entire applied force to the hole.
To see the missing load path, idealize the culet as a coplanar hole region plus a surrounding contact annulus. With a hydrostatic chamber pressure p and axial resultant Fg​ carried by the gasket, its force balance is
F=pAh​+Fg​.
(35)
If the stipulated chamber pressure is 5.40GPa, the hole carries only 42.4N and the gasket carries 957.6N. These are model loads, not measurements. Real gasket deformation and anvil elasticity alter the local contact stress; the scalar balance cannot predict p without additional information. This is why internal pressure calibration matters even when applied force is accurately known.
Ruby pressure scale (Δλ=λR1​​−λR1​,0​)
Words: 1k Articles: 4
Diamond anvil cell OurBigBook.com
The ruby pressure scale converts a shift of a ruby fluorescence spectral line into pressure. Excitation light produces a fluorescence emission spectrum; fitting its R1​ line gives a wavelength λR1​​. The reference λR1​,0​ must be measured or assigned at specified reference pressure and temperature. The difference Δλ is an observable; interpreting it as pressure requires a pressure calibration and suitable stress conditions.
The original 1972 report found sharp R1​,R2​ emission shifting toward lower photon energy as pressure increased; it tentatively associated broadening with nonhydrostatic conditions.[ref] In use, excitation rejection, a calibrated wavelength axis and a fitted background matter because leakage or background can move an apparent peak. A brighter trace improves counting statistics but does not alone establish a correct pressure scale.
Ruby R-line shift (ΔE=hcΔ(1/λ))
Words: 163
Ruby pressure scale OurBigBook.com
The ruby R-line shift compares the same emission feature under two conditions. It is distinct from the Stokes shift, which compares absorption and emission features. In ruby, chromium ions in the corundum crystal provide the electronic transitions; compression changes their local environment and transition energies.[ref]
For consistently defined vacuum wavelengths, the reciprocal relation gives
Δ(1/λ)=λ0​+Δλ1​−λ0​1​=−λ0​(λ0​+Δλ)Δλ​.
(36)
Thus a positive wavelength shift means a negative reciprocal shift, and E=hc/λ gives lower photon energy; h is the Planck constant and c the speed of light. For spectroscopic wavenumber, use vacuum wavelength and keep that convention consistent. A calibration specified in air wavelength must retain its convention or be converted consistently. The reciprocal relation is nonlinear: a line exactly linear in Δλ is not exactly linear in Δ(1/λ).
For a purely mathematical check with chosen vacuum wavelengths λ0​=700.0nm and Δλ=2.0nm, the reciprocal shift is −40.7000cm−1. The small-shift approximation −Δλ/λ02​ gives −40.8163cm−1, about 0.286% too large in magnitude. These chosen values illustrate the conversion; they are not measured ruby lines or an additional pressure calibration.
Ruby calibration against sodium chloride
Words: 187
Ruby pressure scale OurBigBook.com
The 1975 experiment mixed powdered sodium chloride and 0.5%-chromium ruby in a 4:1 volume ratio. An Inconel gasket, initially 0.15mm thick with a 0.3mm hole, held the powder and 4:1 methanol–ethanol. At 25∘C, X-ray diffraction rings on film 12cm away gave salt compression; a reference equation of state assigned pressure. After decreasing load, they waited at least five hours and bracketed diffraction exposures with R1​ readings to check drift.[ref]
The recommended linear slope was 2.740GPanm−1, with a 95% fit confidence interval of ±0.016GPanm−1, to 19.5GPa. Reference-scale systematic measurement uncertainty remained separate. Above about 10.4GPa the medium was only quasihydrostatic; separate range fits checked consistency.[ref]
The logical chain is compression to reference pressure, paired with optical shift, then a fitted response. X-ray diffraction supplies the reference comparison during calibration; subsequent ruby readings transfer that scale to other samples. The reference equation of state is therefore part of the meaning of the reported pressure. Changing it can move all calibrated readings together, even if the optical measurements repeat perfectly. A regression residual tests agreement with the chosen reference within the sampled conditions; it cannot independently certify that reference.

Ruby pressure scale OurBigBook.com
Construct a synthetic local calibration to show the calculation independently of the historical data. Choose reference pairs (Δλi​,pi​)=(1.00,2.69),(2.00,5.42),(3.00,8.09), with shifts in nm and pressures in GPa. The reference zero is already subtracted. Treat the shifts as exact for this fit and give the three reference pressures equal weights. Minimizing the ordinary least squares objective
S(a)=∑i​(pi​−aΔλi​)2
(37)
and setting its derivative to zero gives
a=∑i​(Δλi​)2∑i​Δλi​pi​​=14.0037.80​=2.70GPanm−1.
(38)
The regression residuals are (−0.01,0.02,−0.01)GPa. Their weighted moment ∑i​Δλi​(pi​−aΔλi​) vanishes, as required by the least-squares normal equations. An unknown reference offset requires fitting an intercept instead; forcing it to zero can bias the slope. If shift errors matter, this elementary fit is insufficient.
Use the local measurement model
p=aD,D=λ−λ0​−kT​(T−T0​).
(39)
Here p denotes pressure relative to the reference, a is calibrated sensitivity, and kT​ is a local wavelength sensitivity to temperature at fixed pressure. Choose a=2.70GPanm−1, kT​=0.010nmK−1 and a reading λ−λ0​=2.00nm at T=T0​. The inferred pressure is 5.40GPa. These coefficients and readings are stipulated, not measured ruby constants. With the same pressure, a 10K increase in temperature would add 0.100nm to the shift in this model; neglecting it would overestimate pressure by 0.270GPa.
Assign independent standard uncertainties ua​=0.020GPanm−1, uλ​=u0​=0.010nm and uT​=0.50K for the temperature difference. Here ua​ is an independently assigned calibration uncertainty, not an estimate from the regression residuals above; treat kT​ as exact in this example. First-order propagation of uncertainty follows by differentiating the measurement model:
dp=Dda+adλ−adλ0​−akT​d(T−T0​),
(40)
up2​=D2ua2​+a2(uλ2​+u02​+kT2​uT2​).
(41)
The four standard contributions are 0.0400,0.0270,0.0270,0.0135GPa, giving up​=0.0569GPa. This is a standard uncertainty, not automatically a 95% interval. Correlated reference and loaded wavelength readings require the corresponding covariance term; common wavelength-axis drift may cancel in their difference. Uncertain kT​, nonzero T−T0​, model inadequacy and unresolved deviatoric stress require a broader budget. Taking more optical readings reduces some random errors while leaving a common reference-scale error.
Nonhydrostatic stress in ruby pressure measurement
Words: 243
Ruby pressure scale OurBigBook.com
A single optical shift represents pressure only to the extent that the calibration's mechanical and thermal conditions apply. Under hydrostatic stress, all directions have the same compressive normal stress. Under deviatoric stress, differently oriented ruby grains can respond differently; spatially varying pressure can also superpose shifted lines. These mechanisms can produce different optical signals at equal mean pressure.[ref]
The 2001 account describes scanning local line positions and measuring line width over an extended region. The former resolves spatial differences; the latter supplies a rapid warning.[ref]
Neither a broadened line nor a narrow one uniquely determines the stress tensor. Instrument resolution, temperature variation and unresolved overlapping signals can also affect width. A small observed region can have a narrow line while differing from another region. Compare locations, reference traces and instrument settings before treating width as evidence for a particular mechanical explanation. These are proposed diagnostic checks, not additional historical controls attributed to the 1975 experiment.
Temperature is another independent input. A useful local expansion is Δλ≃sp​p+sT​(T−T0​): one measured shift cannot determine both unknowns. Measure or control temperature, or supply a second independently calibrated observable. The coefficients need not remain constant across a large range. Even when a pressure sensitivity transfers over some temperatures, the reference line, line width and practical readout quality can change.
The historical high-temperature account reports degrading pressure measurement quality above about 300∘C.[ref]
